newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's new bond more than covers 1996 debt needs.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's new bond more than covers 1996 debt needs.

text.p: Mexico's placement of a 20-year bond issue, increased in size to $1.0 billion on Tuesday, more than covers the federal government's foreign debt-refinancing needs for this year, economists said.
Moreover, the deal fits in with Mexico's strategy of replacing short-term debt with longer-term securities and could improve its overall fiscal position, they said.

"That covers their requirements for 1996. It is a good move since it is replacing short-term debt with long-term debt," said Enrique de la Torre, director of fixed-income analysis with Bankers Trust in Mexico City.
On Tuesday, joint lead managers Goldman Sachs International and Merrill Lynch International said the issue was increased by $250 million from the previously announced $750 million.
The pricing was also improved to yield 445 basis points over U.S. Treasuries from the previously indicated range of 450 to 462.5 basis points.

The Mexican Finance Ministry said in a statement that it was aiming to consolidate its position in international markets, and brighten the prospects for future placement by the public and private sectors.
"The timing is right. We are at a point in time where people seem to have a higher comfort level with Mexico," said Morgan Stanley senior economist Ernest "Chip" Brown.
During the past two months, Mexico has placed a six-year, yen-denominated issue worth about $640 million, and a eight-year, $675 million bond denominated in German marks.
Those issues were placed to help pay back a $1.5 billion dual Cetes/Libor note coming due in November.
By placing a $1.0 billion issue on Tuesday, Mexico may have started to tackle the $1.4 billion the United Mexican States will need to refinance in 1997.
Economists said that with the federal budget almost in balance, the proceeds of the 20-year issue could be used for refinancing more expensive debt.
"It certainly doesn't hurt to accumulate a war chest," said Brown.
The government appears to be ready to loosen its fiscal and monetary policy during the rest of the year.

J.P. Morgan noted in a recent report that the government's tight first-half spending policy gives its scope to loosen up. Recent estimates indicate that about 60 percent of the year's total government spending will occur in the second half, it said.
Monetary policy has also eased lately. Moreover, the monetary base traditionally increases sharply before year-end.
"There is certainly still plenty of both peso and dollar debt that is expensive stuff," said Brown.

"It would be better to refinance that. When you expand the money supply at Christmas time maybe the way to do it is to retire some of those Cetes and rely instead on some of this cheap and very long-term foreign debt. It makes more sense in terms of fiscal policy," he said.
The 20-year bond is the second global issue that Mexico has placed this year. In May, it placd a $1.75 billion 30-year bond issue at 552 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
